1101.event_title: The Lady and the Unicorn tapestries show the five senses
1101.place: Woven probably in Flanders; now in the Musée de Cluny, Paris, France
1101.event: Around 1500 a set of six large tapestries known as The Lady and the Unicorn was woven, probably in Flanders, for a patron whom historians identify from its coats of arms as a member of the Le Viste family. Five of the tapestries are understood to show the five senses, sight, hearing, taste, smell and touch, each with a lady accompanied by a lion and a unicorn. The sixth carries the inscription À mon seul désir, meaning to my only desire, and its meaning is still debated; the set now hangs in the Musée de Cluny in Paris.
1101.explanation: The set is one of the best-known works of medieval art, and it gathers all five senses around a single figure before naming one only desire beyond them.
1101.tie_back: The kural says that all the joys of the five senses are found together in one beloved woman, and the tapestries likewise gather sight, hearing, taste, smell and touch around one lady and crown them with a panel addressed to an only desire.
1101._accuracy_note: Five senses gathered around one woman match the kural closely, but the tapestries are not clearly about romantic love and the sixth panel's meaning is disputed.

1102.event_title: Berlioz writes the Symphonie fantastique for Harriet Smithson
1102.event: In 1827 the young composer Hector Berlioz saw the Irish actress Harriet Smithson play Ophelia in Hamlet in Paris and became infatuated with her, but she did not answer his letters. He poured his feelings into the Symphonie fantastique, first performed on 5 December 1830, in which a recurring melody called the idée fixe represents the beloved. Smithson attended a later performance in 1832, and the two married in October 1833, though they later separated.
1102.explanation: One of the most famous symphonies of the Romantic era grew directly out of a lovesick obsession, and the woman who caused it went on to become the composer's wife.
1102.tie_back: The kural says that ordinary illnesses have cures different from their causes, but love-sickness is healed only by the woman who caused it; Berlioz's long fever of love was answered only when Smithson herself accepted him.
1102._accuracy_note: The cause-and-cure idea fits well, but the marriage did not stay happy, so the cure did not last as the kural implies.

1103.event_title: Edward FitzGerald publishes the Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám
1103.event: In 1859 the English scholar Edward FitzGerald published, anonymously, a small pamphlet of verses freely translated from the Persian quatrains of Omar Khayyám. It attracted almost no notice until Dante Gabriel Rossetti came across it in 1860, after which it became one of the most quoted poems in English. In one quatrain of the first edition the speaker pictures bread, wine, a book of verse and the beloved singing beside him, and says that with these the wilderness is paradise enough; the next quatrain mocks those who long for the paradise to come.
1103.explanation: The poem made a medieval Persian voice famous across the English-speaking world, and its picture of simple happiness beside a loved one became proverbial.
1103.tie_back: The kural playfully asks whether even the heaven of the lotus-eyed god could be sweeter than rest beside one's beloved, and the Rubáiyát likewise says the beloved's company makes a wilderness paradise enough, with no need of a paradise to come.
1103._accuracy_note: Ranking the beloved's company above heaven is very close to the kural, though the poem pictures song in the wilderness rather than sleep on the beloved's shoulder.

1104.event_title: June Carter co-writes Ring of Fire
1104.event: June Carter, of the Carter Family of country musicians, co-wrote the song Ring of Fire with Merle Kilgore, picturing love as a burning ring of fire; she wrote it out of her feelings for Johnny Cash and her worries about his troubled life. Her sister Anita Carter recorded it first, and Cash's own version, recorded in March 1963 with Mexican-style horns, reached number one on the country chart and stayed there for seven weeks. June Carter and Johnny Cash married in 1968.
1104.explanation: The song became one of the best-known love songs in American popular music, and its writer later married the man it was about.
1104.tie_back: The kural marvels at a strange fire that burns when the lover moves away and grows cool when he comes near; June Carter's song likewise pictures love itself as a fire, one that burned through the years before she and Cash were finally together.
1104._accuracy_note: Love pictured as fire matches the kural's image, but the song describes falling into the flames rather than a fire that cools when the lovers are together.

1105.event_title: Marc Chagall paints Birthday after Bella's visit
1105.event: On Marc Chagall's birthday, 7 July 1915, Bella Rosenfeld, the young woman he was about to marry, came to his room in Vitebsk bringing flowers and food as birthday gifts. Chagall painted the scene as Birthday, in which he floats up from the floor and bends backwards through the air to kiss her while she holds the bouquet. The couple married later that same month, and the painting is now in the Museum of Modern Art, New York.
1105.explanation: The painting became one of the best-known images of joyful love in modern art, showing a happiness so complete that it lifts the lover off the ground.
1105.tie_back: The kural says the beloved's embrace gives delight just as each longed-for thing does at the very moment it is wanted, and Bella arrived on Chagall's birthday with exactly the gifts of the day, filling his room with a joy he could only paint as flight.
1105._accuracy_note: The right joy arriving at the right moment fits, but the kural describes the constant gift of the beloved's embrace rather than one special day.

1106.event_title: Fanny Osbourne nurses Robert Louis Stevenson back from illness
1106.place: Monterey and San Francisco, California, United States
1106.event: In August 1879 the Scottish writer Robert Louis Stevenson crossed the Atlantic and the American continent in cheap emigrant conditions to join Fanny Van de Grift Osbourne, the American woman he loved, arriving in Monterey thin and unwell. In early 1880 he fell gravely ill, and Fanny, who had divorced her first husband in December 1879, took him into her home and nursed him. They married in San Francisco on 19 May 1880, and she cared for his fragile health for the rest of his life.
1106.explanation: The journey nearly ruined Stevenson's health, yet it gave him the wife who became his lifelong nurse and companion.
1106.tie_back: The kural says that every time the lover is close to his beloved, his wilting life puts out fresh shoots; Stevenson, worn down to skin and bone, was nursed back to life by the woman he had crossed the world to reach.
1106._accuracy_note: Life revived through the beloved's care is a good match, though the kural speaks of the joy of her touch rather than literal nursing through illness.

1107.event_title: Carl Larsson publishes Ett hem (A Home)
1107.event: In 1889 the painter Carl Larsson and his wife Karin, also an artist, were given a small cottage at Sundborn, which they enlarged and transformed into their family home, with Karin designing and weaving many of its textiles. From 1894 Carl painted everyday life there in a series of watercolours, published in 1899 as the book Ett hem (A Home). The pictures of the family's self-made home became a model for Swedish interior decoration, and the house is now a museum.
1107.explanation: The book turned a modest, hand-made family home into a national ideal of comfort and warmth.
1107.tie_back: The kural compares the beloved's embrace to the contentment of living in one's own home and eating what one has earned after sharing it, and the Larssons' Sundborn home, built and furnished by their own hands and shared with the world through Carl's pictures, shows that contentment in real life.
1107._accuracy_note: The home made and shared by a loving couple fits the kural's simile, but the kural's subject is the beloved's embrace, which the book shows only indirectly through family life.

1108.event: The Austrian painter Gustav Klimt painted The Kiss, an image of a couple locked in an embrace, in oil on canvas with gold leaf. It was first shown at the Kunstschau exhibition in Vienna in 1908, and the Austrian state bought it there for 25,000 kronen. It is regarded as the high point of Klimt's Golden Period and hangs in the Belvedere museum in Vienna.
1108.explanation: The painting became one of the best-known images of love in Western art.
1108.tie_back: The kural praises an embrace so close that not even a breath of wind can pass between the two lovers, and Klimt's couple are painted so tightly enfolded that they seem to become a single shape.
1108._accuracy_note: A close, mutual embrace is exactly the kural's subject; the painting is an artwork rather than an event in the lovers' own lives.

1109.event_title: Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton remarry
1109.event: The film stars Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton first married in Montreal in 1964 and divorced in 1974. About sixteen months later, on 10 October 1975, they quietly remarried beside the Chobe River in Botswana while on holiday there, and the news came out a few days afterwards. The second marriage lasted less than a year.
1109.explanation: Their partings and reunions made them one of the most talked-about couples of the twentieth century.
1109.tie_back: The kural names quarrel, reconciliation and reunion as the fruits of love, and Taylor and Burton's return to each other after their divorce is a famous real-life case of falling out and coming back together.
1109._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the cycle of falling out and reuniting fits, but the kural means a brief playful sulk within a happy love, while this was a real divorce and the reunion did not last.

1110.event_title: Will and Ariel Durant write The Story of Civilization together
1110.event: Will Durant met Ariel when he was her teacher at the Ferrer Modern School, and they married in 1913. She began as his research aide on The Story of Civilization, a many-volume history of the world, became his collaborator, and from the seventh volume onward was credited as co-author. In 1968 they won the Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction for Rousseau and Revolution; Ariel died on 25 October 1981 and Will less than two weeks later.
1110.explanation: The Durants' history became one of the most widely read popular histories of the twentieth century, and it was the work of a marriage as much as of one author.
1110.tie_back: The kural says love keeps revealing something new, just as each new piece of learning shows how much more there is to know; the Durants joined their marriage to a lifetime of learning, volume after volume, until both lives ended within days of each other.
1110._accuracy_note: Love and endless learning growing together fits the kural's simile well, though the kural is about love itself feeling ever new, not about a couple studying together.
